newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-JONES POISED TO MAKE BOTH TRACK AND FIELD HISTORY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JONES POISED TO MAKE BOTH TRACK AND FIELD HISTORY.

text.p: - A soft smile spreads over American sprint queen Marion Jones's face when a visitor mentions Florence Griffith Joyner's seemingly impregnable 100 metres world record.
Griffith Joyner clocked 10.49 seconds back in 1988, a time recognised as a world record, although statisticians add the rider "probably wind-assisted".
"I think it can be done," says Jones. "And in the future, it might be done again, and I hope that I am one of those people who get a chance to go after it."
Once a teenage prodigy, she has re-emerged from four years of college basketball and a twice-broken left foot to collect the American women's 100 metres and long jump titles.

Track historians see another Wilma Rudolph, the 1960 triple gold medal sprinter, as the 1.78-metre tall Jones prepares for the women's 100 metres, long jump and 4x100 metres relay at her first world championships starting in Athens this week.
Others look to the future and see a fleeting Jones travelling at speeds and jumping distances never before attained by a woman.

"If she stays on the track, she's going to be one of the greatest females to ever put a pair of shoes on," says John Smith, who coached France's Marie-Jose Perec to the women's 200 and 400 metres title at last year's Atlanta Olympics and has leading men's 100 metres contenders Ato Boldon and Maurice Greene at this year's world championships.

"I think she can run 10.6, 21.3 and jump 25 feet (7.62 metres)," says Smith, giving Jones world records in the 200 metres and long jump. "And from that, she probably will run 10.5 and 21.0. She's capable of doing that."
Her coach, Jamaican-born Trevor Graham, fully believes Jones can some day break the world record in three events -- the women's 100, 200 and long jump.
For now, the goal is a more realistic 10.7 seconds. A similar progression in the 200 metres and long jump must wait for more training.

"She had never been taught," explains Graham, although Jones as a 15-year-old produced times of 11.14 and 22.58 for her California high school. She could have been a relay alternate on the 1992 U.S. Olympic team after finishing fifth in the 100 and fourth in the 200 at the American trials but declined.
Jones agrees fully with Graham's assessment of her running technique.

"When I was younger, and in my first two years in college, I was running off being a pure athlete," says the University of North Carolina graduate. "I never learned the fundamentals of running and jumping.
"When you run so fast at 13, 14 and 15, nobody ever spends any time. They are so impressed that you beat everybody that they don't feel anything needs to be changed.
"Since I have been with Trevor, I feel like I'm in elementary school again. I'm learning the basics."
The lessons are coming fast although she and Graham have worked together only since the early spring.
Along with reshaping the bulk she acquired as a basketball player, they have rebuilt her 100 metres race.

"She didn't understand the race at all," says Graham. "She wasn't cycling properly. Her hands were incorrect. The way she leans forward when she runs..she leans too forward...her head...the whole works."
The quick fix has produced five sub-11 second performances this year and a stunning personal best of 6.93 metres in the long jump as she overtook Jackie Joyner-Kersee at the U.S. championships.

"When you are proving something to yourself, you will do anything it takes to reach your goal," says Jones. "It could have been Carl Lewis in the lane next to me (in the U.S. 100-metre final). I was going to run my best."
Olympic champion Gail Devers missed the final, citing injury, but conquered Jones at Lausanne, clocking a season's best 10.89 seconds to Jones' 10.90.
Two days later, Jones, who claimed she lost form in the Lausanne race, gained revenge in Oslo to even the slate.
Now the American champion draws world champion Gwen Torrence in Athens.

A wild card entry made the clash possible as Torrence missed the U.S. trials due to injury. Devers, the world women's 100 metres hurdles champion, can run that event and the relay also as a wild card competitor.
Graham singles out fellow-Jamaican Merlene Ottey and Torrence as the 100 metres favourites because of their vast experience.
"I would rather be considered as one of the new generation sprinters who popped on the scene and will contend," says Jones.
It might have different, she says, had she been able to compete in the Atlanta Olympics. That was to have been her coming-out party.

"It put a sink in my stomach," she says of the roller-coaster ride of her emotions at the Games. One moment there was joy as she watched her fiancee, C.J. Hunter, compete in the shot. Then, depression as she realised she was not competing.
"If I had the time, and didn't have the unfortunate injuries, I really believe I could have been out there," she says.

Now she is healthy, and happy. There are no basketballs to pick up, no college papers to write or classes to attend. Athletics is now her livelihood, and she and Hunter will be in Athens as team mates.
"I'm here, and I'm here to stay," says Jones. "My spirit is fresh, just bubbling with happiness.

"Being compared, and being put in the same category with Gail and Merlene, athletes who have so much tradition and medals behind them, is really an honour. But you forget about that when you get out there with them. I'm trying to make my own history."
